 Douglas County midterm voter turnout is highest to date
 by Wulfe Wulfemeyer 
 Wulfe Wulfemeyer/Lawrence Times County Clerk Jamie Shew (seated at left at the table) shares voter turnout statistics with Douglas County Commissioners Patrick Kelly, Erica Anderson, Shannon Reid, Karen Willey and Gene Dorsey and County Administrator Sarah Plinsky during the county canvass on Nov. 16, 2026. Many of the people in attendance were board workers who volunteered many hours to assist voters and the elections office. 
 Share this post or save for later 
 Jamie Shew, the Douglas County clerk and elections officer, said folks never stopped voting while polls were open on Election Day — even if that meant stringing a polling place with Christmas lights when the power was out.
 Evergy was doing work in Vinland, leaving the community without power on Nov. 3.
 “We never stopped voting,” Shew said.
 The machines ran on battery backups, and the main office sent universal power sources to the polling location. As it got darker, county maintenance folks brought generators and put up string lights so voters could find the entrance.

 Erica Anderson, county commissioner, said she voted in Vinland and the lights created a “magical experience.”
 Please support 
The Lawrence Times!

 “So many people do vote in person in Vinland, and so you want to know that your polling place is still there and not change that last minute,” she said, commending the elections office.
 Commissioners met with county staff Monday for the canvass, where they certify the results of the election. No commissioner decisions changed the outcomes of any races in Douglas County.
 Shew said this was the county’s fourth largest election to date, and it was the highest turnout ever for a gubernatorial election. 
 Wulfe Wulfemeyer/Lawrence Times Jamie Shew 
 County residents cast 51,201 ballots. The county has 81,651 registered voters, meaning there was a 62.7% voter turnout. That total registration number is up from 80,215 registered in the August primaries . 
 Turnout was 71% in the November 2024 presidential election, and it was 57.9% in the 2022 midterms. 
 Incumbent District 4 County Commissioner Gene Dorsey lost to newcomer Democrat Ethan Spurling in both the primary and the general election, after running a write-in campaign for the latter. Shew said Dorsey put in an affidavit for his write-ins to be counted, which totaled 493.
 Incumbent Anderson won the District 5 county commission seat over her libertarian opponent, Kirsten Kuhn.
 Lawrence voters also opted for an increase and extension to the city’s transit sales tax.
 Douglas County was the only county in Kansas to vote against a proposed constitutional amendment — 64% of voters against, with 36% for — which redundantly establishes that people who are not citizens cannot vote. As that was a statewide question, the amendment passed.
 See the Lawrence Times Election 2026 page to read more about the outcomes of local, state and federal races at this link .
 Misinformation campaigns or misunderstandings?
 Shew said there was a higher incident rate than normal of people who were registered to vote in another Kansas county attempting to vote in Douglas County, at 244.
 Those voters were largely 18- to 24-year-olds who saw something online that told them they could vote anywhere in Kansas as long as they were registered, Shew said. While other states operate that way, you have to vote in the county where you reside in Kansas.
 Shew wasn’t sure if it was a misinformation campaign that led them astray or do-gooders with the wrong information. As a swing state, Kansas captured national attention during this election cycle that it hasn’t previously.
 “We had phone calls from lots of different groups that were across the country and never operated in Kansas that were giving out wrong information because they were used to working in the states without the rule,” Shew said. “And so we had to contact some of these groups to be like, ‘No, no, no, Kansas doesn’t work that way.’”
 Still, Shew said the 18- to 24-year-old voter turnout was particularly good for a governor election.
 Wulfe Wulfemeyer/Lawrence Times A board worker looks at voter turnout by precinct during the canvass. 
 The ballots cast in the wrong county became provisional ballots, which are used to record a vote when questions about the voter’s eligibility must be resolved through the canvass process.
 This year, Shew’s office counted 1,237 of the 1,763 provisional ballots it received. That means 526, or about 29.8%, of the provisional ballots were not counted. The office didn’t count any of the provisional ballots from voters registered in other Kansas counties.
 Shew also addressed misinformation about the audit with commissioners.
 Douglas County has done an audit since 2018, Shew said. They always audit 1% of the precincts, and 10% of close races. In this election cycle, there were four close races: governor, secretary of state, attorney general and House District 117.
 “There’s a lot of rumors that this was a recount, it was a sign that something was wrong,” he said. “It was not.”
 Ultimately, they reviewed 21,837 ballots, or 42.6% of the ballots. They found only four ballots where someone made a checkmark that wasn’t in the oval a voter is meant to color in.
 Change in voter behaviors
 Shew and his office counted 26,611 advance votes total. That’s in line with past elections, but voter behavior changed: 18,295 people voted in person; 9,917 people requested mail-in ballots, and the elections office got 8,988 back, marking a 90.6% return rate. 
 Shew said the number of mail ballot requests, which usually hovers around 15,000, was low.
 “That increase in in-person wasn’t necessarily a lot of new voters,” Shew said. “They were people who normally vote in a polling place that were voting early for the first time, or they were mail voters voting early for the first time.”
 He said the change is due to delays in the United States Postal Service.
 When someone mails a ballot in Lawrence, it goes to a Kansas City post office facility for processing before returning to Lawrence. Shew said that, on average, the process takes seven to nine days.
 Douglas County is the only county in Kansas that pays for a tracking system to see where ballots are. Shew said it paid off, as Ed Healy, Douglas County deputy clerk, drove the Kansas City facility “crazy” asking about ballots held up in processing.
 He also said the Lawrence post office worked hard to get those ballots in during the last few days.
 Wulfe Wulfemeyer/Lawrence Times Douglas County Commissioners Patrick Kelly, Erica Anderson, Shannon Reid, Karen Willey, Gene Dorsey and County Administrator Sarah Plinsky hear election results during the county canvass. 
 Eudora splits on sales tax
 Shew said it will take counting provisional ballots Monday afternoon to see how a sales tax vote in Eudora will shake out after a polling snafu.
 The vote was to continue a sales tax rate, already levied twice, to support the construction of the Community Center. This time, city staff wanted to redirect the tax revenue to public safety .
 On Oct. 24, the elections office found out that a poll worker was handing out advance ballots incorrectly. As a result, 11 voters had the wrong ballots.
 Five Eudora voters got township ballots and didn’t vote on the tax question. Four Eudora voters got the wrong city ballot but still voted on the tax question. Two township voters weighed in on the question when they shouldn’t have.
 “This is the only instance of that. This is not a systemic issue,” Shew said. “This was a board worker that didn’t understand the instructions at that moment.”
 He said it wasn’t the worker’s fault, and he aims to make the process clearer in the future. In the meantime, there’s not much they can do.
 “The law is very clear that once the voter has voted that ballot, it’s voted,” Shew said. 
 To complicate matters, the Election Day total was split evenly: 1,150 saying “yes” and 1,150 saying “no.”
 Shew said the city could put the question on a spring ballot, and the elections office would “work with them” on the cost.
